title: Astera Genomics — Security Briefing: Private/VPC & Egress Strategy

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-18
Start: 15:38 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lin Zhou (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Nair (CISO, Astera), Marcus Hale (Head of Infra), Lena Ortiz (DevOps), Omar Khan (Compliance)

Summary / auto notes (auto generated, may be fuzzy):
- Focus on private deployment and VPC isolation, egress control and KMS options.
- Discussed SOC 2 implications for hosted vs private key stores and audit log retention.
- Action items captured at end.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone thanks for making time, I'm Samir with Redwood Inference. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Priya: Hi Priya here, CISO at Astera. Marcus and Lena on.
[00:08] Marcus: Marcus here, yes.
[00:10] Samir: Great. Lin and Marta from our side, SEs. We planned a security rundown: network isolation, ingress/egress, and key management. Sound right?
[00:18] Priya: Yep. Also want to dig into audit trails and retention — we have SOC2 upcoming so we need specifics.
[00:23] Lin: Understood. I'll try to map the network flows and where logs and keys live.
[00:27] Marta: I'll pick up questions about RBAC and SSO mapping.
[00:30] Marcus: One constraint up front: we run private cluster in our colo and will not allow outbound internet except to a small set of destinations — company policy.
[00:38] Lin: Ok that's common. There are a few patterns: 1) fully private with egress proxy/NAT and explicit allowlist 2) VPC with PrivateLink to Redwood control plane 3) On‑prem airgapped with file handshake for model updates. We'll walk through tradeoffs.
[00:50] Priya: What's the difference for audit and SOC2 if keys are in Redwood KMS vs our HSM?
[00:55] Samir: Good question. High level: if you use Redwood hosted KMS (we integrate with cloud KMS providers), we provide evidence of encryption-in-transit and at-rest, and we include relevant controls in our SOC2 report. If you require customer-controlled keys, we support bring‑your‑own‑KMS via customer KMS or HSM; that pushes the responsibility for key lifecycle and some controls to you, and we provide encrypted keywrap flows and logs.
[01:12] Priya: So we would need to see key rotation/usage logs and HSM attestations. Can you provide that level of detail?
[01:16] Lin: We can share a key usage audit feed — it contains timestamped operations for encrypt/decrypt/key-access. For HSM we record key wrap/unwrapped events. Some of the low-level attestation artifacts (e.g., HSM vendor certs) we can reference as links in the compliance pack.
[01:29] Omar: Is there an option for FIPS‑140‑compliant HSM?
[01:32] Marta: Yes, we integrate with FIPS validated KMS providers and can work with on‑prem HSMs via PKCS#11 bridges.
[01:38] Marcus: For network, we need to avoid egress to the public internet. What's the minimal set of external endpoints Redwood needs to talk to?
[01:44] Samir: We'll produce an allowlist. Typical needs: control plane endpoints for telemetry and configuration, container image registries for updates (unless you pull images into your registry), model artifact fetching if you want hosted model pulls, and optionally metrics/tracing endpoints. If you're on Dedicated or Private, you can route telemetry to your own endpoints.
[02:02] Lena: We would prefer telemetry inbound to our ELK stack. Can Redwood forward logs instead of pushing out to your SaaS?
[02:07] Lin: Definitely. For Private deployment we can configure log shippers to push to your internal endpoints — or we can write logs to S3 compatible storage in your VPC.
[02:15] Priya: Retention: we need 7 years for certain logs? Is that possible?
[02:18] Marta: Long retention is supported if the storage is under your control — we don't force deletion. For hosted storage we generally follow a default retention, but for Private/VPC you manage retention policy.
[02:26] Marcus: How do you handle ingress — do you put a public LB in front of inference nodes?
[02:31] Lin: For Private we recommend an internal load balancer (ILB) in a private subnet, with a bastion jump host for admin actions. Ingress typically goes through the customer's API gateway or an internal reverse proxy — we don't require a public LB.
[02:45] Marcus: And for mTLS?
[02:47] Samir: mTLS is supported between services. We can integrate with customer PKI for certs and mutual TLS for control plane connections.
[02:53] Priya: For RBAC and SSO, can we map our Azure AD groups directly to Redwood roles?
[02:57] Marta: Yes, SAML/OIDC mapping is supported. You can map groups to roles and we support SCIM for provisioning. There will be a connector for group-to-role sync.
[03:05] Omar: Any record of admin actions — who rolled a model, who changed a rollout policy?
[03:10] Lin: All control plane operations are audit logged with actor identity, IP, and request details. For Private, logs can be shipped to your SIEM.
[03:17] Priya: Can you show a network example?
[03:20] Lin: (screen share) Here's a typical setup: customer VPC with private subnets for inference nodes, internal LB, NAT/egress proxy in a controlled subnet, customer KMS in a private subnet or external HSM connected via a bridge, and a dedicated management plane that can be peered or provisioned through PrivateLink.
[03:40] (few seconds of screen flicker)
[03:44] Lena: If we use an egress proxy, does Redwood support HTTP CONNECT tunneling for model downloads?
[03:49] Lin: Yes, the agent supports proxy env vars and authenticated proxies. For large model downloads we recommend pulling artifacts into a local registry to avoid live egress.
[03:57] Marcus: What about IP allowlisting for peering — can we pin to static IPs or CIDR ranges?
[04:02] Samir: We can provide stable ranges for control plane IPs; for Dedicated/Private we can establish VPC peering or PrivateLink to avoid public IPs entirely.
[04:10] Priya: SOC2 — do you provide a dedicated whitepaper describing control mappings for data classification and encryption?
[04:14] Samir: Yes, will share SOC2 summary, control mappings, and the sections relevant to encryption/key mgmt and logging. We'll redact client-specific details.
[04:22] Omar: How do you prove separation of duties for audit?
[04:25] Marta: Our RBAC model includes separation of role capabilities and we can export role-to-action mappings for auditors. For Private installs the management plane can be deployed in a separate VPC so you can demonstrate isolation.
[04:35] Marcus: In terms of firewalling, we need egress control to an outbound proxy that also does TLS inspection. Will Redwood tolerate TLS interception for egress?
[04:44] Lin: If you intercept TLS at the proxy, the agent needs to trust your proxy CA; we support custom CA bundles so the runtime accepts the proxy's certificate. There are caveats with cert pinning for some upstream services but generally it's supported.
[04:57] Priya: What about log integrity — are logs signed or tamper-evident?
[05:01] Lin: We support writing logs to append-only stores and can include signed log entries (HMAC) for additional integrity. For the highest assurance we suggest shipping to a customer-managed WORM store.
[05:12] Marcus: Network latency — adding an egress proxy or private peering will add hops. What's the latency impact?
[05:17] Samir: Typical added latency for an egress proxy in same region is 5–15ms for the handshake; token lookups and model runtime are still dominant. We can run a small benchmark in your environment during PoC.
[05:30] Lena: For runtime secrets, where do embeddings live? Are they stored in plain S3?
[05:34] Marta: Embeddings and cache can be stored encrypted at rest and in a customer controlled bucket; caches can also be in‑memory only. We recommend encrypting any persisted vectors with KMS keys you control.
[05:45] Priya: Are there known compliance blockers for our use case (clinical genomics)?
[05:49] Samir: Clinical data increases sensitivity. The main blockers are data residency and ensuring PII/PHI handling controls. For Private deployments in your region with customer‑managed KMS and strict egress allowlist these are typically addressed. We can map controls to your SOC2/ISO requirements and support any additional attestation needs.
[06:05] Marcus: Ok let's talk timeline — if we go PoC in January, what do you need from us?
[06:09] Lin: We'll need network ranges, list of allowed egress destinations, a staging VPC or access details, and the key management preference.
[06:15] Samir: We'll assemble a checklist and share it.
[06:18] (wrap up)
[06:20] Samir: Quick recap: Redwood to share SOC2 pack and whitepapers; Lin to create network diagram; Astera to provide egress whitelist and confirm KMS stance. We'll reconvene after docs are exchanged to schedule PoC kickoff.
[06:36] Priya: Sounds good, thanks.
[06:38] Marcus: Thanks all.
[06:40] Samir: Thanks — end call.
